title: Bits, Bytes & Number Reference
html:
Every bit-width that shows up across the stack, and what it's actually used for.

WidthUsed forPossible values
8-bitOne octet of an IPv4 address (e.g. the "192" in 192.168.1.1)2⁸ = 256 (0–255)
16-bitPort numbers; each field in a UDP header (source port, dest port, length, checksum)2¹⁶ = 65,536 (0–65,535)
32-bitAn entire IPv4 address; TCP sequence/acknowledgement numbers2³² ≈ 4.3 billion
128-bitAn entire IPv6 address2¹²⁸ ≈ 3.403 × 10³⁸

16 binary cells, each either 0 or 1 → 2¹⁶ total combinations ≈ 65,000 usable port numbers, split across the reserved (0–1023), registered (1024–49151), and dynamic/ephemeral (49152–65535) ranges.

Header sizes worth memorizing

HeaderSize
UDP header8 bytes (4 × 16-bit fields)
TCP header20 bytes minimum
IP packet header20 bytes
MAC address48 bits (12 hex digits)

Data rate units

UnitValue
1 kbps1,000 bits/sec
1 Mbps1,000,000 bits/sec
1 Gbps10⁹ bits/sec

Address space scale, side by side

IPv4 — 32 bit

2³² ≈ 4.3 billion total addresses — already exhausted globally, which is the core reason NAT and IPv6 both exist.

IPv6 — 128 bit

2¹²⁸ ≈ 3.4 × 10³⁸ addresses — for scale, enough to assign a unique address to every grain of sand on Earth many times over.
